notes: A scanline is 228 colour clocks: 68 of horizontal blank (HBLANK) followed by 160 visible pixels (x = 0..159). The 6507 runs at the colour clock divided by 3, so a line is 76 CPU cycles and 1 cycle = 3 pixels. NTSC colour clock is 3.579545 MHz and PAL about 3.546894 MHz. A frame is 262 lines (19912 cycles) in NTSC or 312 lines (23712 cycles) in PAL.

Address decoding: the TIA answers when A12 = 0 and A7 = 0, so $0000-$007F and their mirrors ($0100-$017F, ...). Writes look at A0-A5 (registers $00-$2C, repeated every $40); reads look only at A0-A3 (collision and input registers, repeated every $10). Programs commonly read them at $00-$0D (DASM vcs.h) or at the mirror $30-$3D.
A write reaches the TIA on the last cycle of the writing instruction (cycle 3 of STA zp, 4 of STA abs or STA zp,X, 6 of STA (zp),Y). Use that cycle when computing beam position.

Horizontal positioning: the position of an object is set by when its RESxx strobe is written, counted in CPU cycles from the start of the line. If the write happens in cycle N (0-based, N = the cycle of the data write), the player's first pixel is at x ~ 3*N - 68 + 5 and the missile or ball at x ~ 3*N - 68 + 4 (measured on Gopher2600: N = 23 gives player 6 and missile/ball 5; N = 25 gives 12 and 11). Towers explains the +5: the counter reset, start decode and latch add up to a few clocks. Positions come in steps of 3 pixels, hence the 15-pixel coarse loops plus HMxx/HMOVE fine motion.

A strobe does not move the object on the line where it is written: the new position first shows on the next line (Stella guide). Strobes written during HBLANK do not follow the formula: the guide says the object goes to the left edge; Gopher2600 puts a player at pixel 3 and a missile or ball at pixel 2 when no HMOVE has been used on that line, with different values if HMOVE is active. The exact value is emulator-derived and unconfirmed on hardware.

Typical positioning routine: WSYNC, then a loop that subtracts 15 from the wanted x each pass (5 cycles = 15 pixels), a RESxx strobe when the loop ends, and an HMxx value from the remainder (-8..+7, i.e. high nibble of HMxx) applied by HMOVE right after the next WSYNC. Loop offsets depend on the exact code, so verify the result in an emulator.

HMOVE comb: an HMOVE strobed right after WSYNC extends HBLANK by 8 colour clocks (Towers), so the first 8 visible pixels of that line are black. If every kernel line uses HMOVE the black column is constant; games hide it with a border or by using HMOVE only on lines that do not matter. A late HMOVE (see HMOVE) avoids the extension.

Object priority with PFP = 0: P0/M0, then P1/M1, then PF/BL, then background. With PFP = 1: PF/BL, then P0/M0, then P1/M1, then background. SCORE mode only changes which player colour the playfield takes in each half (Stella guide).

Collision latches are set whenever the pixels of two objects overlap, whatever their colours or priority, and are only cleared by a write to CXCLR. There are 15 pairs, read two at a time in D7 and D6 (Stella guide).

Strobe registers (WSYNC, RSYNC, RESP0/1, RESM0/1, RESBL, HMOVE, HMCLR, CXCLR) act on any write and ignore the data. A read of the same low address returns a collision or input register (the read map is separate) and does not strobe anything.

Collision and input registers drive only D7 (and D6 for collisions); the other bits are not driven by the TIA and are normally seen as leftovers of the data bus. The usual advice is to mask or to use BIT, which puts D7 in N and D6 in V.

The TIA exists in several board revisions. Gopher2600 exposes options for revision-dependent behaviour (late RESPx after HMOVE, early scan counter, RESPx near the end of HBLANK depending on temperature), so exact cycle behaviour at these edges is not fully specified in the primary documents; use hardware tests when it matters.

Audio: two channels clocked at the colour clock / 114 (about 31.4 kHz NTSC, which is twice per scanline). AUDCx selects a polynomial counter or divider combination, AUDFx divides the clock by 1-32 and AUDVx sets the volume 0-15.

Frame structure used by the Stella guide: 3 lines VSYNC, 37 lines VBLANK, 192 lines of picture and 30 lines of overscan (NTSC, 262 total); PAL 3 + 45 + 228 + 36 = 312. VBLANK D1 is set outside the picture. See tv.json.

Playfield: 20 bits per half, each 4 pixels wide, taken from PF0 bits 4-7, PF1 bits 7-0 and PF2 bits 0-7 in that order. The right half repeats the left (CTRLPF bit 0 = 0) or mirrors it (bit 0 = 1). There is no enable bit: write 0 to PF0-PF2 to hide it.
Because the TIA ignores A6 on writes beyond the register range and A8+ entirely, the same register appears at several addresses; indexed stores that wrap into page 0 can hit the TIA by accident.

registers.name: VSYNC
registers.description: Bit 1 = 1 starts the vertical sync signal and 0 stops it; the other bits are ignored. The TV needs at least 3 lines of VSYNC to start a new frame. The TIA does not count lines: keeping the frame at 262 (NTSC) or 312 (PAL) lines is the program's job. Usual sequence: set bit 1, run 3 WSYNCs, clear it.
registers.timing: The signal follows the write; it is normally started right after a WSYNC so it begins at the start of a line.
issues: VSYNC only produces the sync pulse; VBLANK ($01) is what blanks the picture.
A frame with a line count that is not 262/312, or that changes between frames, makes the picture roll or lose lock; Stella reports the detected scanline count.
A stray indexed store that wraps into the TIA mirrors can write VSYNC by accident (see the TIA notes about address decoding).
registers.example:
lda #2
  sta VSYNC
  sta WSYNC
  sta WSYNC
  sta WSYNC
  lda #0
  sta VSYNC

registers.name: VBLANK
registers.summary: Vertical blank, paddle dump and input latch control.
registers.description: Bit 1 (D1) = 1 blanks the video output (black), 0 shows it; the program turns it on for the vertical blank / overscan lines and off before the visible area. Bit 6 (D6) = 1 enables the latches on the joystick fire inputs INPT4/INPT5 (once the fire button pulls the line low the bit stays 0 until D6 is cleared); D6 = 0 makes them follow the pin. Bit 7 (D7) = 1 'dumps' the paddle input capacitors to ground, forcing INPT0-INPT3 to read 0; clearing D7 lets the capacitors charge so the paddle position can be measured by counting scanlines until the INPT bit goes to 1.
registers.timing: The blanking follows the write, so writing it mid-line blanks only the rest of the line.
issues: Bit 1 only blanks the video output; it is not the same as VSYNC.
With D6 = 1 the fire inputs INPT4/INPT5 are latched: once the line goes low the bit stays 0 until D6 is cleared (writing D6 = 0 also resets the latches to 1).
Writing D7 = 1 grounds INPT0-INPT3 (paddle capacitors discharged); clear it to let them charge.
registers.example:
lda #%11000010   ; dump paddles, latch fire buttons, blank screen
  sta VBLANK
  ...
  lda #%01000000   ; un-dump, keep latch, picture on
  sta VBLANK

registers.name: WSYNC
registers.description: Any write halts the 6507 (RDY pulled low) until the TIA reaches the leading edge of the next horizontal blank. The next instruction starts at CPU cycle 0 of the following line. The value written is ignored.
registers.timing: Release happens at the start of the next line. Measured on Gopher2600: a WSYNC whose write lands in cycle 72, 74 or 75 resumes at cycle 0 of the next line, so a write in cycle 75 gives only a very short stall but still ends on the next line boundary; a write that lands in cycle 0 of a line (or after cycle 75) waits a whole extra line.
issues: The stall consumes whatever remains of the line, so code between two WSYNCs has to fit in 76 cycles or the second WSYNC will wait an extra line.
WSYNC is a write-only strobe: a read of address $02 returns the CXP0FB collision register and does not stall the CPU, so use STA (or STX/STY), not LDA or BIT.
Kernels that need more than one TIA write per line, or that race the beam, count cycles with NOP/branch loops instead of using WSYNC mid-line.
registers.example: sta WSYNC     ; cycle 0 of next line after this

registers.name: RSYNC
registers.description: Any write resets the horizontal sync counter. The Stella guide says it is meant for chip testing; the hardware notes say the reset takes effect only after a short delay and warn that the details need more investigation. Rarely used.
registers.timing: Unverified: the delay between the write and the counter reset is not given in the sources used.
issues: Unverified: a line shortened by RSYNC has a non-standard length and TV behaviour is unspecified.
Unverified: since positioning counters run from the same horizontal counter, RSYNC can change where later RESxx strobes land; emulators differ here, so test on hardware.

registers.name: NUSIZ0
registers.summary: Player 0 / Missile 0 number-size and missile size.
registers.description: Bits 5-4 = missile 0 width: 00 = 1 clock, 01 = 2, 10 = 4, 11 = 8. Bits 2-0 = player 0 copies and size: 000 one copy; 001 two copies close (16 pixels between starts); 010 two copies medium (32 apart); 011 three copies close (16 apart); 100 two copies wide (64 apart); 101 one double-width copy (16 pixels wide); 110 three copies medium (32 apart); 111 one quad-width copy (32 pixels wide). Bits 7-6 and 3 are unused. The same bits 2-0 also decide how many copies of the missile are drawn: the Stella guide says the missile counter uses the same decodes as the player, so the missile repeats with the player copies (its width comes from bits 5-4).
registers.timing: Copy positions are fixed counter decodes (Towers): the close copy starts 16 pixels after the main one, the medium copy 32 and the far copy 64.
issues: Unverified: changing NUSIZ in the middle of a line (after a copy has started) is used to cut copies or retime them; the effect depends on the TIA revision and is not specified in the sources used.
Double and quad width are stretched versions of the same 8 bits; the player start is delayed by the stretch (Towers discusses the extra delay but the exact offsets were not confirmed here).
With RESMPx set the missile follows the player; its alignment to the player depends on the player's size.
registers.example:
lda #%00110011   ; 8-clock missile, three close copies
  sta NUSIZ0

registers.name: NUSIZ1
registers.summary: Player 1 / Missile 1 number-size and missile size.
registers.description: Bits 5-4 = missile 1 width: 00 = 1 clock, 01 = 2, 10 = 4, 11 = 8. Bits 2-0 = player 1 copies and size: 000 one copy; 001 two copies close (16 pixels between starts); 010 two copies medium (32 apart); 011 three copies close (16 apart); 100 two copies wide (64 apart); 101 one double-width copy (16 pixels wide); 110 three copies medium (32 apart); 111 one quad-width copy (32 pixels wide). Bits 7-6 and 3 are unused. The same bits 2-0 also decide how many copies of the missile are drawn: the Stella guide says the missile counter uses the same decodes as the player, so the missile repeats with the player copies (its width comes from bits 5-4).

issues: Unverified: changing NUSIZ in the middle of a line (after a copy has started) is used to cut copies or retime them; the effect depends on the TIA revision and is not specified in the sources used.
Double and quad width are stretched versions of the same 8 bits; the player start is delayed by the stretch (Towers discusses the extra delay but the exact offsets were not confirmed here).
With RESMPx set the missile follows the player; its alignment to the player depends on the player's size.

registers.name: COLUP0
registers.description: Bits 7-4 = hue (0-15), bits 3-1 = luminance (0-7); bit 0 is ignored, so there are 8 brightness levels. Colours player 0 and missile 0, and the left half of the playfield in CTRLPF SCORE mode. The meaning of the hue values differs between NTSC, PAL and SECAM (see tv.json); on SECAM only luminance bits 3-1 choose the colour.
issues: Hue 0 is a grey scale. On PAL, hues 0, 1, 14 and 15 are all grey (as in common PAL palettes; not checked in a primary document).
The colour/B&W switch is only readable in SWCHB bit 3; software normally picks a grey-scale palette when it reads 0.
Writing a colour register mid-line changes the colour from the next pixel on, which allows colour changes inside a line.
registers.example:
lda #$1E
  sta COLUP0

registers.name: COLUP1
registers.description: Same format as COLUP0. Colours player 1 and missile 1, and the right half of the playfield in SCORE mode.
issues: See COLUP0.

registers.name: COLUPF
registers.description: Same format as COLUP0. Colours the playfield (except in SCORE mode) and the ball.
issues: See COLUP0.

registers.name: COLUBK
registers.description: Same format as COLUP0. Colour of the background, shown where no other object is.
issues: Rewriting COLUBK every line gives horizontal colour bars.
registers.example:
sta WSYNC
  sta COLUBK

registers.name: CTRLPF
registers.description: Bit 0 REF: reflect the playfield (the right half is the left half mirrored instead of repeated). Bit 1 SCORE: the left half of the playfield takes the colour of player 0 and the right half that of player 1. Bit 2 PFP: playfield and ball are drawn in front of players and missiles. Bits 5-4: ball width (00 = 1 clock, 01 = 2, 10 = 4, 11 = 8).
issues: Priority with PFP = 0: P0/M0, P1/M1, PF/BL, background. With PFP = 1: PF/BL, P0/M0, P1/M1, background.
SCORE colours switch at the middle of the line (pixel 80).
Unverified: how SCORE interacts with PFP when playfield pixels overlap a player is not described in the sources used.
registers.example:
lda #%00000101   ; reflect + playfield on top
  sta CTRLPF

registers.name: REFP0
registers.description: Bit 3 = 1 reverses the horizontal order of the player 0 graphics (bit 0 drawn leftmost instead of bit 7). Other bits are ignored. Applies to every copy of the player.
issues: Reflection is applied while drawing, so it can be changed between lines. Unverified: changing it while the player is being drawn is timing-sensitive.
registers.example:
lda #8
  sta REFP0

registers.name: REFP1
registers.description: Same as REFP0 for player 1.
issues: See REFP0.

registers.name: PF0
registers.summary: Playfield pixels 0-3 (4 bits), left to right.
registers.description: Only bits 7-4 are used. Bit 4 is the leftmost playfield block on screen, then bits 5, 6 and 7. Each playfield bit is 4 colour clocks wide; the 20 bits of PF0 (high nibble), PF1 and PF2 cover the left 80 pixels, and the right half repeats or mirrors them (CTRLPF bit 0).
registers.timing: Left half: PF0 is drawn at pixels 0-15 (colour clocks 68-83), PF1 at 16-47 and PF2 at 48-79. Right half: PF0 at pixels 80-95, PF1 at 96-127 and PF2 at 128-159 (reflected copies come in reverse order: PF2, PF1, PF0 with the bits reversed).
issues: Bit order differs: PF0 uses bits 4-7 left to right, PF1 uses bits 7-0 and PF2 uses bits 0-7. This is the most common source of playfield bugs.

Unverified (derived from the pixel positions above, not measured): to give the right half a different pattern, write the new PF0 between about CPU cycle 28 and 49, PF1 between about 39 and 54, PF2 between about 50 and 65 of the line.
Unverified: a write that lands while a playfield pixel is being drawn may show the old or the new value depending on write latency and TIA revision.
registers.example:
lda #%11110000
  sta PF0     ; four blocks at the left edge

registers.name: PF1
registers.description: All 8 bits used. Bit 7 is the leftmost of the 8 blocks, bit 0 the rightmost (reverse of PF2's order).
registers.timing: Left half pixels 16-47 (clocks 84-115); right half pixels 96-127 (clocks 164-195).
issues: See PF0 for bit order and mid-line rewrite windows.

registers.name: PF2
registers.description: All 8 bits used. Bit 0 is the leftmost of the 8 blocks, bit 7 the rightmost (same direction as PF0).
registers.timing: Left half pixels 48-79 (clocks 116-147); right half pixels 128-159 (clocks 196-227).
issues: See PF0 for bit order and mid-line rewrite windows.

registers.name: RESP0
registers.description: Any write sets the horizontal position of player 0 from the colour clock at which the write lands; the data is ignored. Position cannot be written directly. The new position first shows on the next scanline.
registers.timing: Position (screen x = 0..159) when written in CPU cycle N of the line (N = the cycle in which the data write happens): x ~ 3*N - 68 + 5 for players and 3*N - 68 + 4 for missiles and the ball. This matches the 5-clock delay in Towers and was measured on Gopher2600 (N = 23 gives player 6, missile and ball 5). For writes during HBLANK the guide says the object goes to the left edge; Gopher2600 uses pixel 3 for a player and 2 for a missile or ball when HMOVE has not been used in that line.
issues: Positions come in steps of 3 pixels (one CPU cycle); the usual divide-by-15 loop reaches 15-pixel steps and HMxx plus HMOVE give the remaining -8..+7.

Unverified (emulator-derived): the left-edge column reached from HBLANK strobes and the extra delay when HMOVE is active in that line differ between TIA revisions; leftmost positions are normally reached with HMOVE after a coarse placement.
The player's main copy is not generated by the strobe itself (Towers): the new position first draws on the following line; strobing twice in one line suppresses the main copy.
registers.example:
sta WSYNC
  SLEEP 20
  sta RESP0   ; position depends on cycle count

registers.name: RESP1
registers.description: Any write sets the horizontal position of player 1 from the colour clock at which the write lands; the data is ignored. Position cannot be written directly. The new position first shows on the next scanline.
registers.timing: Position (screen x = 0..159) when written in CPU cycle N of the line (N = the cycle in which the data write happens): x ~ 3*N - 68 + 5 for players and 3*N - 68 + 4 for missiles and the ball. This matches the 5-clock delay in Towers and was measured on Gopher2600 (N = 23 gives player 6, missile and ball 5). For writes during HBLANK the guide says the object goes to the left edge; Gopher2600 uses pixel 3 for a player and 2 for a missile or ball when HMOVE has not been used in that line.
issues: Positions come in steps of 3 pixels (one CPU cycle); the usual divide-by-15 loop reaches 15-pixel steps and HMxx plus HMOVE give the remaining -8..+7.

Unverified (emulator-derived): the left-edge column reached from HBLANK strobes and the extra delay when HMOVE is active in that line differ between TIA revisions; leftmost positions are normally reached with HMOVE after a coarse placement.
The player's main copy is not generated by the strobe itself (Towers): the new position first draws on the following line; strobing twice in one line suppresses the main copy.
registers.example:
sta WSYNC
  SLEEP 20
  sta RESP1   ; position depends on cycle count

registers.name: RESM0
registers.description: Any write sets the horizontal position of missile 0 from the colour clock at which the write lands; the data is ignored. Position cannot be written directly. The new position first shows on the next scanline.
registers.timing: Position (screen x = 0..159) when written in CPU cycle N of the line (N = the cycle in which the data write happens): x ~ 3*N - 68 + 5 for players and 3*N - 68 + 4 for missiles and the ball. This matches the 5-clock delay in Towers and was measured on Gopher2600 (N = 23 gives player 6, missile and ball 5). Unverified (emulator-derived): the left-edge column reached from HBLANK strobes and the extra delay when HMOVE is active in that line differ between TIA revisions; leftmost positions are normally reached with HMOVE after a coarse placement.
While RESMPx is set the missile is locked to its player and RESMx has no visible effect.
registers.example:
sta WSYNC
  SLEEP 20
  sta RESM0   ; position depends on cycle count

registers.name: RESM1
registers.description: Any write sets the horizontal position of missile 1 from the colour clock at which the write lands; the data is ignored. Position cannot be written directly. The new position first shows on the next scanline.

registers.name: RESBL
registers.description: Any write sets the horizontal position of the ball from the colour clock at which the write lands; the data is ignored. Position cannot be written directly. The new position first shows on the next scanline.
registers.timing: Position (screen x = 0..159) when written in CPU cycle N of the line (N = the cycle in which the data write happens): x ~ 3*N - 68 + 5 for players and 3*N - 68 + 4 for missiles and the ball. Unlike the other objects, a RESBL strobe starts the ball immediately (Towers), so it can be retriggered several times in one line.
registers.example:
sta WSYNC
  SLEEP 20
  sta RESBL   ; position depends on cycle count

registers.name: AUDC0
registers.description: Bits 3-0 select the sound type (Stella guide table): 0 = output held at 1 (silence), 1 = 4-bit poly, 2 = divide by 15 then 4-bit poly, 3 = 5-bit poly then 4-bit poly, 4 and 5 = pure tone (divide by 2), 6 = pure tone divide by 31, 7 = 5-bit poly then divide by 2, 8 = 9-bit poly (white noise), 9 = 5-bit poly, 10 = pure tone divide by 31, 11 = last 4 bits set to 1 (constant), 12 and 13 = pure tone divide by 6, 14 = pure tone divide by 93, 15 = 5-bit poly divide by 6. Bits 7-4 are unused.
registers.timing: The audio clock is the colour clock divided by 114 (about 31.4 kHz NTSC), twice per scanline.
issues: Pure-tone frequency ~ 31400 / ((AUDF + 1) * divider) Hz in NTSC, with the divider from the list above (the guide quotes a 30 kHz base clock).
On SECAM, silence must be made with AUDV = 0, not AUDC = 0 (Stella guide).
registers.example:
lda #12
  sta AUDC0     ; div 6 pure tone

registers.name: AUDC1
registers.description: Same as AUDC0 for channel 1.
issues: See AUDC0.

registers.name: AUDF0
registers.description: Bits 4-0 divide the audio clock by AUDF0 + 1 (0 = no division, 31 = divide by 32). Combined with the divider chosen in AUDC.
issues: Steps are coarse at the high end; build note tables per AUDC type.

registers.name: AUDF1
registers.description: Same as AUDF0 for channel 1.
issues: See AUDF0.

registers.name: AUDV0
registers.description: Bits 3-0 = volume 0-15; 0 gives no output. Changing it quickly is used to play digital samples at the cost of CPU time.
issues: Unverified: whether volume changes take effect at once or only on audio-clock boundaries; programs that play samples through AUDV rely on it being fast.

registers.name: AUDV1
registers.description: Same as AUDV0 for channel 1.
issues: See AUDV0.

registers.name: GRP0
registers.description: 8 bits of pixel data for player 0; bit 7 is the leftmost pixel (unless REFP0 is set). With VDELP0 set, a write to GRP0 only updates the 'new' value; the 'old' value is displayed until GRP1 is written (writing GRP1 copies the new GRP0 into the delayed register). Each pixel is one colour clock wide (more with NUSIZ stretch).
issues: With VDELP0 = 1 the player shows the old copy of GRP0, which is loaded when GRP1 is written (not when GRP0 is written).
Writing GRP0 while the player is being drawn changes the remaining pixels of that line (used by wide-sprite kernels; timing-sensitive).
registers.example:
lda #%00111100
  sta GRP0

registers.name: GRP1
registers.description: Same as GRP0 for player 1. Writing GRP1 also copies the current GRP0 into the delayed GRP0 register and ENABL into the delayed ENABL register, whether or not VDELP0/VDELBL are set (confirmed in Stella's TIA model).
issues: A write to GRP0 likewise copies GRP1 into the delayed GRP1 register (used by VDELP1).

registers.name: ENAM0
registers.description: Bit 1 = 1 enables missile 0 (drawn with COLUP0, width set by NUSIZ0). Other bits ignored. If RESMP0 bit 1 is set, the missile is hidden regardless of ENAM0.
issues: The missile has no vertical-delay register.

registers.name: ENAM1
registers.description: Same as ENAM0 for missile 1.

registers.name: ENABL
registers.description: Bit 1 = 1 enables the ball (drawn with COLUPF, width from CTRLPF). With VDELBL set the ball shows the delayed value, which is updated when GRP1 is written.
issues: The delayed ENABL copy is made on every GRP1 write.

registers.name: HMP0
registers.description: Bits 7-4 hold a signed 4-bit value for the fine motion applied at the next HMOVE: $70 = 7 pixels left, $00 = none, $80 = 8 pixels right; $10..$70 move left 1-7 and $80..$F0 move right 8-1 (Stella guide). Bits 3-0 are ignored.
issues: The motion registers must not be modified during the 24 CPU cycles after an HMOVE (Stella guide and Towers).
Values are only used when HMOVE is strobed; HMCLR zeroes all five.
To convert a remainder to the nibble, positioning routines usually apply EOR and shifts so that the sign convention matches.
registers.example:
lda #$70   ; 7 pixels left
  sta HMP0

registers.name: HMP1
registers.description: Bits 7-4 hold a signed 4-bit value for the fine motion applied at the next HMOVE: $70 = 7 pixels left, $00 = none, $80 = 8 pixels right; $10..$70 move left 1-7 and $80..$F0 move right 8-1 (Stella guide). Bits 3-0 are ignored.
issues: The motion registers must not be modified during the 24 CPU cycles after an HMOVE (Stella guide and Towers).
Values are only used when HMOVE is strobed; HMCLR zeroes all five.
To convert a remainder to the nibble, positioning routines usually apply EOR and shifts so that the sign convention matches.
registers.example:
lda #$70   ; 7 pixels left
  sta HMP1

registers.name: HMM0
registers.description: Bits 7-4 hold a signed 4-bit value for the fine motion applied at the next HMOVE: $70 = 7 pixels left, $00 = none, $80 = 8 pixels right; $10..$70 move left 1-7 and $80..$F0 move right 8-1 (Stella guide). Bits 3-0 are ignored.

To convert a remainder to the nibble, positioning routines usually apply EOR and shifts so that the sign convention matches.

  sta HMM0

registers.name: HMM1
registers.description: Bits 7-4 hold a signed 4-bit value for the fine motion applied at the next HMOVE: $70 = 7 pixels left, $00 = none, $80 = 8 pixels right; $10..$70 move left 1-7 and $80..$F0 move right 8-1 (Stella guide). Bits 3-0 are ignored.
issues: The motion registers must not be modified during the 24 CPU cycles after an HMOVE (Stella guide and Towers).
Values are only used when HMOVE is strobed; HMCLR zeroes all five.
To convert a remainder to the nibble, positioning routines usually apply EOR and shifts so that the sign convention matches.
registers.example:
lda #$70   ; 7 pixels left
  sta HMM1

registers.name: HMBL
registers.summary: Horizontal motion value for the ball.
registers.description: Bits 7-4 hold a signed 4-bit value for the fine motion applied at the next HMOVE: $70 = 7 pixels left, $00 = none, $80 = 8 pixels right; $10..$70 move left 1-7 and $80..$F0 move right 8-1 (Stella guide). Bits 3-0 are ignored.

registers.name: VDELP0
registers.description: Bit 0 = 1 draws player 0 from the delayed copy of GRP0, which is loaded with the current GRP0 value whenever GRP1 is written. Used to update GRP0 and GRP1 in an interleaved way and show both on the same line (48-pixel sprites).
issues: Mechanism confirmed in Stella: a GRP1 write loads delayed GRP0 (and delayed ENABL); a GRP0 write loads delayed GRP1.
In 48-pixel kernels both VDELP0 and VDELP1 are set.
registers.example:
lda #1
  sta VDELP0
  sta VDELP1

registers.name: VDELP1
registers.description: Bit 0 = 1 draws player 1 from the delayed copy of GRP1, loaded when GRP0 is written.
issues: See VDELP0.

registers.name: VDELBL
registers.description: Bit 0 = 1: the ball enable comes from the delayed ENABL register, which is loaded when GRP1 is written.
issues: The displayed ball ignores new ENABL writes until a GRP1 write copies them.

registers.name: RESMP0
registers.description: Bit 1 = 1 locks missile 0 to the centre of player 0 and hides it; clearing the bit releases it, and it then moves independently from that position (Stella guide).
issues: The exact pixel offset of the 'centre' depends on the player's size; the sources used give no table, so check with an emulator.
Typical use: keep a bullet inside the player, then release it on fire.

registers.name: RESMP1
registers.description: Same as RESMP0 for missile 1 and player 1.
issues: See RESMP0.

registers.name: HMOVE
registers.description: Any write applies the HMxx motion values to the five objects, each by its signed amount. It has to be strobed right after a WSYNC, at the start of HBLANK: the TIA then also extends the blank by 8 colour clocks, which hides the first 8 pixels of the line (the 'HMOVE comb').
registers.timing: Valid at CPU cycle 0 of a line (just after WSYNC). Stuffed clocks arrive every 4 colour clocks for up to about 21 CPU cycles, which is why the HMxx registers must not be touched for 24 cycles afterwards (Towers).
issues: HMOVE comb: each line where HMOVE is strobed in the normal window starts with 8 black pixels.

Late HMOVE (Towers): an HMOVE written around CPU cycle 74 of the previous line clears the HBLANK extension, so there is no comb; motion is then only to the left, by 8 + the usual value (so HM = -8 gives no movement and all other objects shift further left). Only cycle 74 is described in the source; neighbouring cycles were not confirmed here.
Unverified: HMOVE in the middle of the visible line can move objects to the right by about 1 pixel per 4 clocks (stated as unverified by Towers).
Unverified: RESxx strobes while the HMOVE motion is still rippling behave differently from normal.
registers.example:
sta WSYNC
  sta HMOVE
  ; motion applied; leftmost 8 pixels blank on this line

registers.name: HMCLR
registers.description: Any write sets HMP0, HMP1, HMM0, HMM1 and HMBL to 0. Use after positioning so later HMOVE strobes do not keep moving objects.
issues: Needed when HMOVE is strobed every line and objects should not drift.
registers.example: sta HMCLR

registers.name: CXCLR
registers.description: Any write resets all 15 collision latches to 0.
issues: Normally done once per frame near the end of vertical blank (Stella guide); read the latches after the picture has been drawn.
Collisions are based on overlapping pixels of objects, regardless of colour (even an object coloured like the background still collides).
registers.example: sta CXCLR

registers.name: CXM0P
registers.summary: Collision: missile 0 and player 1 (bit 7), missile 0 and player 0 (bit 6).
registers.description: Bit 7 = 1 if missile 0 and player 1 have collided (any pixel overlap) since the last CXCLR; bit 6 = 1 if missile 0 and player 0 have. Bit 7 and bit 6 hold two of the 15 collision latches; they stay set until CXCLR. Latches are set by pixel overlap, independent of colour and priority. The other bits are not driven by the TIA (they usually show data-bus leftovers), so mask or use BIT.
issues: Latched, not live: use CXCLR to clear.
Do not compare the whole byte; bits 5-0 are not driven (use BIT: bit 7 goes to N, bit 6 to V).
registers.example:
bit CXM0P
  bmi .hit7   ; bit 7
  bvs .hit6   ; bit 6

registers.summary: Collision: missile 1 and player 0 (bit 7), missile 1 and player 1 (bit 6).
registers.description: Bit 7 = 1 if missile 1 and player 0 have collided (any pixel overlap) since the last CXCLR; bit 6 = 1 if missile 1 and player 1 have.   bvs .hit6   ; bit 6

registers.summary: Collision: player 0 and playfield (bit 7), player 0 and ball (bit 6).
registers.description: Bit 7 = 1 if player 0 and playfield have collided (any pixel overlap) since the last CXCLR; bit 6 = 1 if player 0 and ball have. The playfield collides even if its colour equals the background.

registers.name: CXPPMM
registers.summary: Collision: player 0 and player 1 (bit 7), missile 0 and missile 1 (bit 6).
registers.description: Bit 7 = 1 if player 0 and player 1 have collided (any pixel overlap) since the last CXCLR; bit 6 = 1 if missile 0 and missile 1 have. registers.name: INPT0
registers.description: Bit 7 reads 1 once the paddle capacitor has charged past the threshold and 0 while it is lower or dumped (VBLANK D7 = 1). To read a paddle: set VBLANK D7 for a while to discharge, clear D7, then count scanlines until bit 7 becomes 1; the count grows with the resistance. The same inputs are the column inputs of keypad controllers. The other bits are not driven.
registers.timing: Unverified: the longest charge time (full paddle sweep) is longer than a frame in typical references, so many games read over several frames or clip the range.
issues: The bit is analogue; noisy paddles flicker near the threshold, so filter the readings.
While VBLANK D7 = 1 the bit reads 0.
Keypads use INPT0/INPT1/INPT4 (left port) and INPT2/INPT3/INPT5 (right port) as column inputs.
registers.example:
bit INPT0
  bmi .charged

registers.name: INPT4
registers.description: Bit 7 = 0 while the fire button of controller 0 is pressed, 1 when released. With VBLANK D6 = 1 the input is latched: once it goes low the bit stays 0 until D6 is cleared (the Stella guide describes the latch). The other bits are not driven; the input is also a keypad column input.
issues: Active low: 0 = pressed.
Joystick directions are not on the TIA: they are in SWCHA ($0280) on the RIOT.
Programs that use the latch for 'press to start' must clear it (D6 = 0 then 1) before the next press.
registers.example:
lda INPT4
  bpl .firePressed

registers.name: INPT5
registers.description: Bit 7 = 0 while the fire button of controller 1 is pressed, 1 when released. With VBLANK D6 = 1 the input is latched: once it goes low the bit stays 0 until D6 is cleared (the Stella guide describes the latch). The other bits are not driven; the input is also a keypad column input.
